summary: Instagram is where nearly all the audience is: most videos get 500-1,400 views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly get under 60 views. The best performers are short, punchy 'X doesn't do what you think, it only does Y' explainers on familiar gadgets (clap switch, gyro robot, line follower), and posts with a surprising or relatable angle earn shares and saves. The weakest are plain 'How does X work? 🤔' question titles, which got no Instagram traction (or were never posted there) and almost no YouTube views, and the newest videos have very low reach on both platforms.
winningPattern: Instagram-first Hindi Reels about a familiar robot or sensor gadget (clap switch, gyro robot, line follower, IR robot) with a myth-busting hook: 'It doesn't X, it only Y', or a 'without this, the robot falls' consequence hook. Titles are short, in Hinglish, with one emoji. The topic is something makers have built or seen. The clap switch and robot-behavior videos also get some YouTube views, while UV, soil and dustbin topics get shares on Instagram only.
doMore: Post every video to Instagram first, then treat YouTube as secondary and test a separate thumbnail/title there
Use the myth-bust hook 'X doesn't do A, it only does B' or a failure hook like 'Without this, the robot falls'
Make more beginner-project topics: robots, clap switch, line follower, and other Arduino builds people can copy
Add a save or share trigger at the end, like 'Save this for your project' or 'Send this to your maker friend'
Make a part 2 for the best topics (gyro, clap switch) with a new angle instead of repeating the same video
stopDoing: Generic 'Kaise Kaam Karta Hai? 🤔' question titles with no surprising claim
Posting near-duplicate topics (three clap switch, many IR/PIR videos) within weeks of each other
Posting to YouTube only and skipping Instagram
